content: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is the most common pre-malignant lesion of the cervix. It is characterized by atypical squamous cell changes that occur in the transformation zone of the cervix. These changes can be classified as mild, moderate, or severe, depending on the depth of the abnormality, and are categorized as CIN 1, CIN 2, or CIN 3, respectively. The treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia typically involves either local ablation or excision techniques that are associated with lower morbidity. The choice of treatment is determined by the grade and extent of the disease. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of different surgical treatments for CIN. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to November 2012. Additional sources, such as clinical trial registries, abstracts from scientific meetings, and reference lists of included studies, were also reviewed. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared alternative surgical treatments for women diagnosed with CIN. Data collection and analysis were performed independently by two reviewers, who extracted data and assessed the risk of bias. The outcomes of interest included residual disease after follow-up and adverse events. Risk ratios were calculated, and the data were pooled using random-effects model meta-analyses. The surgical techniques evaluated included laser ablation, laser conisation, large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ), knife conisation, and cryotherapy. A total of 29 trials were included in the analysis, testing seven different surgical techniques in various comparisons. The results showed no significant differences in treatment failures, as measured by the persistence of disease after treatment, among the techniques. However, large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) appeared to provide the most reliable specimens for histological examination while being associated with the least morbidity. Compared to laser conisation, LLETZ demonstrated lower morbidity, although not all outcome measures were reported in the trials. There was insufficient data to evaluate the impact of LLETZ on morbidity when compared to laser ablation. In conclusion, the evidence does not indicate a clearly superior surgical technique for the treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in terms of treatment failures or operative morbidity.
